outputs.L1: We demonstrate that the number of renewals up to time \(t\) exhibits distributional fluctuations as \(t \to \infty\), provided that the underlying lifetimes grow at an exponential rate in a distributional sense. This offers a probabilistic explanation for the asymptotic behavior of insertion depth in random trees generated by a bit-comparison strategy from uniform input. We also derive a representation for the resulting family of subsequential limit laws. Our approach further yields rates of convergence.
outputs.L2: We demonstrate that, as \(t\) tends to infinity, the count of renewals by time \(t\) has nontrivial limiting distributional oscillations when the associated interarrival times grow exponentially in distribution. This yields a probabilistic interpretation of the asymptotic behavior of insertion depth in random trees built from uniform data using a bit-comparison rule. In addition, we derive a representation of the corresponding collection of subsequential limit distributions, and our method is capable of providing convergence rates as well.
outputs.L3:
When the lifetimes in a renewal process increase exponentially in distribution, the number of renewals observed up to a fixed time \(t\) does not settle into a single limiting distribution as \(t \to \infty\). Instead, it exhibits distributional fluctuations: along different subsequences of \(t\), different limiting laws may appear. This phenomenon reflects the fact that exponentially growing lifetimes introduce an inherent oscillatory structure into the renewal count, preventing ordinary convergence in distribution.

This renewal-theoretic result provides a probabilistic explanation for the asymptotic behavior of insertion depth in certain random trees. In particular, consider random trees constructed from uniform input by a bit-comparison strategy, where elements are inserted according to successive comparisons of their binary expansions. The depth at which a new item is inserted can be interpreted through a renewal process whose interarrival times correspond to increasingly large lifetime increments. Since these lifetimes grow exponentially in distribution, the insertion depth inherits the same type of asymptotic fluctuation. Thus, the renewal-process analysis explains why the insertion depth does not necessarily converge to a single universal limit, but may instead have different limiting distributions along suitable subsequences.

The authors further develop a representation for the full family of limit laws that can arise in this setting. Rather than identifying only isolated subsequential limits, they describe the possible limiting distributions in a unified way. This representation captures how the limiting law depends on the subsequence along which time tends to infinity, or equivalently on the phase of the underlying logarithmic scale created by exponential growth. As a result, the asymptotic behavior can be understood as a structured family of limits rather than as irregular or accidental non-convergence.

In addition to identifying these limiting laws, the same probabilistic approach can be used to obtain quantitative rates of convergence. That is, it not only describes which subsequential limits occur, but also estimates how quickly the distribution of the renewal count, or the corresponding insertion depth in the random tree model, approaches its limiting form along appropriate subsequences. This makes the method useful both for qualitative asymptotic analysis and for sharper probabilistic approximations.
outputs.L4:
This work studies distributional fluctuations in renewal counting processes in a setting where the underlying lifetimes grow exponentially in distribution. Rather than focusing only on first-order asymptotics, it investigates the finer limiting behavior of the number of renewals and identifies the sources of persistent oscillations that appear after centering and scaling. The analysis is motivated by, and applied to, the insertion depth of random trees constructed from independent uniform input sequences using bit comparisons.

In these random tree models, each inserted item is represented by an infinite binary string, and the depth at which a new item is inserted depends on how many initial bits must be inspected before it can be distinguished from previously inserted items. This depth can be represented in terms of a renewal process whose interarrival times are related to logarithmic transformations of products of random variables. Because these interarrival times exhibit exponential growth in distribution, classical renewal theorems do not directly describe all of the relevant fluctuations. A more refined probabilistic treatment is therefore required.

The paper develops such a treatment by analyzing the renewal count along suitable subsequences. It shows that, although a single ordinary limiting distribution may fail to exist because of arithmetic or oscillatory effects, well-defined subsequential limit laws do arise. These limit laws capture the distributional behavior of the centered renewal count and, consequently, of the insertion depth in the associated random trees. The results clarify why the depth does not simply converge after standard normalization, but instead displays periodic or subsequential asymptotic patterns.

In addition to identifying the limiting distributions, the work establishes convergence-rate estimates. These results quantify how quickly the renewal counts, and hence the insertion depths, approach their subsequential limits. Such rate information strengthens the limit theorems and provides a more precise description of the finite-size behavior of the tree model.

Overall, the text connects renewal theory with the probabilistic analysis of digital random trees. It explains the asymptotic behavior of insertion depth by reducing the problem to renewal counts with exponentially growing lifetimes, proving subsequential convergence results, and deriving rates of convergence. In doing so, it gives a rigorous probabilistic account of the fluctuations observed in random trees generated by bit-comparison from uniform data.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a concise academic abstract for a probability paper about renewal processes with exponentially growing lifetimes and applications to insertion depth in random bit-comparison trees.
counterfactuals.output: We study renewal processes whose interarrival times grow exponentially with the renewal index, a nonstationary regime arising in the analysis of random bit-comparison trees. For a broad class of lifetime distributions, we derive asymptotic estimates for renewal counts, overshoots, and related passage-time functionals, emphasizing the effects of lattice versus nonlattice structure. The results are obtained through a combination of renewal-theoretic arguments, transform methods, and sharp tail estimates adapted to exponentially scaled increments. As an application, we analyze the insertion depth in random trees built by sequential comparisons of binary strings, where successive comparison costs increase geometrically. The limiting behavior of the depth is shown to be governed by the associated exponentially growing renewal process, yielding explicit asymptotics and fluctuation results. These findings provide a probabilistic framework for understanding search and insertion complexity in digital structures with multiplicative cost growth.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the main contribution of a study showing distributional fluctuations in renewal counts as time grows, with consequences for random trees built from uniform inputs.
counterfactuals.output:
The study’s main contribution is to show that renewal counting processes can exhibit persistent **distributional fluctuations** as time tends to infinity: after the usual centering, the renewal count need not converge to one universal limiting law, but may have limits that depend on the arithmetic/phase structure of the underlying inter-renewal distribution.

A key point is that these fluctuations are not just a technical feature of renewal theory. They propagate into models of **random trees built from uniform inputs**—for example, trie-like or split-tree structures—because depths, profiles, or related tree parameters can often be represented through renewal counts. As a result, certain tree statistics may also display oscillatory or subsequential limiting behavior rather than clean convergence to a single asymptotic distribution.

In short, the paper links fine renewal-theoretic fluctuations with observable asymptotic phenomena in random trees, showing that periodic or phase-dependent effects must be accounted for when analyzing such tree models.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a short research-paper blurb explaining how exponential growth of interarrival times leads to subsequential limit laws for renewal counts and insertion-depth asymptotics.
counterfactuals.output:
We study renewal processes whose interarrival times grow exponentially, a regime in which the usual law-of-large-numbers scaling is replaced by logarithmic time scales. If \(S_n=\sum_{k\le n} X_k\) with \(X_k\) increasing on the order of \(e^{ck}\), then the renewal count
\[
N(t)=\max\{n:S_n\le t\}
\]
is typically of order \((\log t)/c\). However, because the last few exponentially large summands dominate the partial sum, the centered count \(N(t)-(\log t)/c\) generally does not converge along the full continuum \(t\to\infty\). Instead, its distribution depends on the fractional position of \(\log t/c\), producing a family of subsequential limit laws indexed by limiting values of \(\{\log t/c\}\). Thus exponential growth converts renewal asymptotics into a log-periodic phenomenon.

These renewal limits provide the probabilistic input for insertion-depth asymptotics in recursively defined structures. The depth of a newly inserted item can often be represented, up to negligible error, as a renewal count evaluated at a size parameter \(t\) proportional to the current number of stored items. Consequently, the depth has leading term \((\log t)/c\), while its fluctuations inherit the same subsequential limits as the underlying renewal process. In particular, full distributional convergence may fail, but along sequences \(t_m\) for which \(\{\log t_m/c\}\to\theta\), the centered insertion depth converges to a non-degenerate law depending on \(\theta\). This yields a precise description of the asymptotic depth profile, including its logarithmic growth rate, bounded fluctuations, and intrinsic periodicity on the logarithmic scale.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you formulate a polished abstract for a theorem connecting renewal theory, distributional convergence along subsequences, and random trees generated by bit comparisons?
counterfactuals.output:
We prove a renewal-theoretic limit theorem for a class of random trees generated by bit comparisons, encompassing digital search trees, tries, and related comparison structures built from independent infinite binary strings. The key observation is that many structural parameters of these trees can be represented, after suitable Poissonization, through renewal sums associated with the logarithms of splitting probabilities. When the underlying renewal process is non-lattice, this representation yields ordinary distributional convergence after centering and scaling. In the lattice case, however, periodic fluctuations persist, and full convergence generally fails. We show that convergence is recovered along subsequences for which the relevant fractional parts converge, and we identify the limiting laws explicitly in terms of renewal limits and the limiting phase.

More precisely, we establish that a broad family of tree functionals admits subsequential weak limits determined by the arithmetic nature of the source distribution. The proof combines renewal theory, analytic depoissonization, and contraction-type arguments for recursive distributional equations arising from the bit-comparison construction. This framework explains the appearance of oscillatory phenomena in random digital trees and provides a unified description of all possible subsequential limits. As an application, the theorem yields refined asymptotics for quantities such as tree depth, path length, collision counts, and comparison costs, clarifying the precise sense in which these parameters converge in distribution and how their limits depend on the binary source.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.output: The paper establishes limit theorems for renewal processes whose successive lifetimes grow exponentially, showing that the renewal count has predictable logarithmic growth and proving precise fluctuation limits after centering and scaling. It also gives quantitative convergence rates—rather than just weak convergence—for these renewal-count approximations, typically in metrics such as Kolmogorov distance. These renewal results are then applied to random tree models, where the depth of a typical node can be represented or approximated by such a renewal count. As a consequence, the paper derives central-limit-type asymptotics and explicit rates of convergence for the distribution of random tree depths.
